customer_question: If our OEM customizes the chipset vendor's stock Bluetooth Profile implementation, does the customized Profile need its own testing, and can we check ahead of time that it won't create an inter-layer inconsistency with our Host QDID?
question_variants: Can we rely on the chipset vendor's own Profile test evidence if we've customized their Profile?
Is there a way to check for Consistency Check problems before committing to full testing?
Can you run a simulation to confirm Invalid=0 with our Host QDID before we test the custom Profile?
actual_issue: The customer's OEM intended to customize the chipset vendor's stock Bluetooth Profile implementation, raising the question of whether the customized Profile needed to be separately tested rather than relying on the vendor's existing Profile test evidence, and whether the resulting combination could be checked for inter-layer inconsistency against the Host QDID before committing to full testing.
plain_english_explanation: If an OEM takes a chip vendor's ready-made Bluetooth feature and modifies it, the vendor's original test results no longer fully represent what the OEM is actually shipping, so the modified version needs to be tested in its own right. Before spending the time and cost on that full test, it's possible to run a quick check using the planned registration's settings to make sure the certification system won't reject the combination outright once everything is submitted -- catching configuration problems early instead of after testing is already complete.
consultant_answer: If the OEM customizes the chip vendor's Profile, testing of that custom Profile is required -- the vendor's own Profile test evidence covers only their stock implementation, not the OEM's customization. After that testing, it is important to confirm early whether the test results and the Host QDID will produce an inter-layer inconsistency (Invalid=0), and this confirmation can be done as a simulation performed by the consultant ahead of committing to the full registration, reducing the risk of discovering an inconsistency only after testing is complete.
decision_logic: A chipset vendor's existing Profile test evidence only covers their unmodified, stock implementation; any OEM customization to that Profile requires its own separate testing, and running an early inter-layer consistency simulation against the intended Host QDID configuration -- before or alongside that testing -- is the appropriate way to catch a potential Invalid result before it surfaces in the formal registration process.
final_recommendation: When an OEM customizes a chipset vendor's stock Profile implementation, plan for separate testing of the customization and request an early inter-layer consistency simulation (Invalid=0 check) against the intended Host QDID configuration before committing to full testing.
risk_if_done_wrong: Assuming the chipset vendor's existing Profile test evidence covers an OEM-customized version of that Profile risks submitting an inadequately-tested registration. Skipping the early Invalid=0 simulation risks discovering an inter-layer inconsistency only after full testing has already been completed, at greater cost and delay.
